title: Example: drawing a simple house

visuals.title: Build the house in this order

stages.name: 1. Plan on a grid
stages.detail: Write down the corner coordinates of the walls, the roof peak and the door before typing any code.

stages.name: 2. Walls
stages.detail: rectangle(left, top, right, bottom) gives the box of the house.

stages.name: 3. Roof
stages.detail: Two line() calls meet at the peak: from the wall's top-left to the peak, and from the peak to the top-right.

stages.name: 4. Door
stages.detail: A small rectangle standing on the bottom edge of the walls, centred.

stages.name: 5. Colour and extras
stages.detail: setfillstyle + floodfill for the walls, a circle for the sun, outtextxy for the label.

visuals.title: The notes' house with red walls, a sun and a label

goal: After this you can plan a drawing on a coordinate grid and turn the plan into graphics.h code: walls, roof, door, window, sun and text.
warmup: Before a mason builds a house in Lahore he does not just start laying bricks: the architect draws a plan with measurements. The same works for a drawing program. If you first write the numbers on paper (where the walls start, how high the roof peak is), the code is easy, and mistakes are easy to find.
definition: A drawing is built from simple shapes placed with coordinates. A house is a rectangle (walls), two lines (roof), a smaller rectangle (door), maybe a circle (sun) and some text. Each shape is one function call, and the order of the calls is the order of drawing. graphics.h is not standard C++. It runs only on a lab PC with Turbo C++ (DOSBox) or Code::Blocks/Dev-C++ plus the WinBGIm library, so the in-page compiler cannot run these programs. The canvas on this page is a simulation that draws what the same calls would draw.
howItWorks: Step 1, plan: the walls are the rectangle from (200, 200) to (400, 350). Step 2, roof: its peak is in the middle above the walls, at x = (200 + 400) / 2 = 300 and y = 120; two lines join the wall's top corners to the peak. Step 3, door: a small rectangle 50 pixels wide centred on x = 300, so it runs from x = 275 to x = 325 and from y = 280 down to the bottom of the walls at y = 350. Step 4, colour: setfillstyle then floodfill with a point just inside the walls. floodfill fills only the closed region that the point is in, so the roof triangle (closed by the walls' top edge) stays unfilled; to colour it too you would call floodfill again with a point inside the roof, for example (300, 160). Step 5: sun and text. Remember y grows downwards: the roof peak has a SMALLER y than the walls. The first sample does only the planning arithmetic as a normal console program (it really runs). The two drawing samples are for Turbo C++ / WinBGIm and are simulated by the canvas.
syntax:
rectangle(200, 200, 400, 350);   // walls: left, top, right, bottom
line(200, 200, 300, 120);        // roof left:  wall top-left  -> peak
line(300, 120, 400, 200);        // roof right: peak -> wall top-right
rectangle(275, 280, 325, 350);   // door: centred, standing on the bottom edge
setfillstyle(SOLID_FILL, RED);   // fill colour for the walls
floodfill(210, 210, WHITE);      // a point inside the walls; border = outline colour
circle(520, 90, 40);             // sun
outtextxy(240, 380, (char*)"My House");   // label below the house

sample.title: Planning the house coordinates

explanation.text: The four numbers of the wall rectangle.
The middle of the wall: (200 + 400) / 2 = 300. The roof peak and the door are centred here.
The peak is 80 pixels ABOVE the top edge, so we SUBTRACT: 200 - 80 = 120 (y grows downwards).
The door is 50 wide, so 25 pixels left of the middle: 275.
25 pixels right of the middle: 325.
The door starts at y = 280 and goes down to the bottom of the walls (350).
Prints the wall corners.
Prints the peak (300, 120): the numbers used in the roof lines.
Prints the door corners; its bottom is the bottom of the walls.

steps.note: peakY = 200 - 80 = 120, higher on the screen than the walls.
The door top is fixed at 280.

Colouring the walls or the sun

mistakes.right: line(200, 200, 300, 120);   // peak ABOVE the wall: smaller y
mistakes.error: No compiler error. The roof points into the house, because y grows downwards.

mistakes.wrong: rectangle(275, 280, 325, 300);   // door floats in the air
mistakes.right: rectangle(275, 280, 325, 350);   // bottom = bottom of the walls
mistakes.error: No compiler error, but the door does not reach the bottom of the walls.

mistakes.wrong: floodfill(210, 210, RED);   // border colour is wrong
mistakes.right: floodfill(210, 210, WHITE);   // the outline is WHITE
mistakes.error: No compiler error. The border colour must be the colour of the outline; with a wrong border the paint does not stop at the walls.

mistakes.wrong:
line(200, 200, 300, 120);
// forgot the right roof line
mistakes.error: No compiler error, but the roof is open on one side.

examTips: Start your answer with a small coordinate plan: walls, peak, door. It gains marks and prevents mistakes.
Know the notes' house program: rectangle for walls, two lines for the roof, rectangle for the door, floodfill, circle for the sun, outtextxy.
The roof peak has a SMALLER y than the wall top. The door bottom equals the wall bottom.
Set the colour before each shape, and the floodfill border colour equals the outline colour.
Mention that the program runs under Turbo C++ or WinBGIm, and that initgraph's path differs between the two.
romanSummary: Ghar banane se pehle coordinates ka plan kaghaz par likhein: walls, roof ki choti, darwaza.
Walls rectangle se, roof do line() se, darwaza chhote rectangle se, sooraj circle se aur text outtextxy se banta hai.
Roof ki choti ka y chhota hota hai kyun ke y neeche ki taraf barhta hai.
Rang bharne ke liye setfillstyle aur floodfill, border ka colour outline wala hi dein.
Yeh programs lab PC par Turbo C++ ya WinBGIm mein chalte hain, page ka canvas sirf simulation hai.

practice.prompt: In the notes' house, which function draws the walls?
How many line() calls make the roof?
practice.hint: The wall's top edge is already drawn by the rectangle.
practice.explanation: One line from the left wall corner to the peak and one from the peak to the right wall corner.

practice.prompt: The walls run from x = 200 to x = 400. Where is the middle (roof peak x)?

Fill the blank to draw a door 50 pixels wide centred on x = 300, standing on the bottom edge y = 350 and starting at y = 280.

rectangle(___, 280, 325, 350);
practice.explanation: The left edge of a door 50 wide centred at 300 is 300 - 25 = 275; the right edge is 325.

practice.hint: A roof peak is higher than the wall top.
practice.explanation: Higher means a smaller y: 120, not 280.

practice.prompt: Why does the program call floodfill(210, 210, WHITE) with WHITE as the last argument?
options: WHITE is the colour of the walls' outline, so the paint stops there
WHITE is the new fill colour
practice.answer: WHITE is the colour of the walls' outline, so the paint stops there
practice.explanation: The walls were drawn with setcolor(WHITE), so the outline is white and floodfill stops at white pixels.

practice.prompt: Write a graphics program that draws a house: walls (100, 200) to (300, 350), a two-line roof with its peak at (200, 120), and a door from (175, 280) to (225, 350).
practice.hint: Walls, then two roof lines meeting at (200, 120), then the door.
practice.explanation: The middle of the walls is (100 + 300) / 2 = 200, which matches the peak x and the centre of the door (175 to 225). Runs on a lab PC; the page only simulates it.

quiz.prompt: What should you do BEFORE writing the code of a drawing?
options: Plan the coordinates on a grid
quiz.answer: Plan the coordinates on a grid
quiz.explanation: A plan with coordinates makes the code simple.

quiz.prompt: Which shape is the sun in the notes' program?
The roof peak is at y = 120 and the wall top at y = 200. Which is higher on the screen?
quiz.explanation: 120 is smaller than 200, so the peak is above the wall top.

quiz.prompt: Which call writes the label under the house?
quiz.explanation: outtextxy(x, y, text) writes text at a position.

quiz.prompt: In initgraph(&gd, &gm, (char*)"C:\\TURBOC3\\BGI"), what is the third argument?
options: The folder holding the BGI driver files (Turbo C++)
quiz.answer: The folder holding the BGI driver files (Turbo C++)
quiz.explanation: Turbo C++ loads its drivers from that folder; WinBGIm does not need it, so an empty string is used.
